PROTACs (Proteolysis-Targeting Chimeras) facilitate the degradation of pathogenic proteins in Alzheimer's Disease by hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_27]. They are heterobifunctional molecules consisting of a moiety that binds the target protein (POI), a linker domain, and a domain that binds an E3 ubiquitin ligase [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_25]. 

Specifically, PROTACs bind to both the E3 ligase and the target protein, forming a ternary complex (PROTAC-POI-E3) [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_25]. This brings the target protein into spatial proximity with the E3 ligase, facilitating ubiquitination and subsequent degradation by the 26S proteasome [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_26]. 

This mechanism is particularly valuable in AD because PROTACs can degrade proteins that lack easily druggable active sites, such as Tau [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_29]. Several PROTACs have been designed to increase the degradation of GSK-3β, and one, PT-65, has shown promise in decreasing Tau hyperphosphorylation *in vitro* and *in vivo* [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_37]. Furthermore, PROTACs like C004019 can cross the blood-brain barrier [HSR2-9-e71631, Chunk_41].

response: The inhibition of O-GlcNAcase (OGA) is considered an attractive therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease (AD) due to reduced O-GlcNAcylation levels observed in AD brains [main (1), Chunk_66]. Specifically, O-GlcNAcylation levels in AD brains were reported to be 22% lower than in healthy brains [main (1), Chunk_66]. Furthermore, hyperphosphorylated tau exhibits four times less O-GlcNAc groups compared to non-hyperphosphorylated tau [main (1), Chunk_66]. reference: Inhibiting OGA reduces the formation of pathological tau and ameliorates neurodegeneration by increasing the O-GlcNAcylation of tau protein.
